Opinion: Now is exactly the time to double down on technical skills

I'm a senior IC who's been in the industry for about a bit less than a decade, mostly at Google and a couple of other FAANGs prior. My superpower has always been deep technical knowledge, and I wanted to see if anyone else has similar feelings about how to thrive in a post-Al tech industry.
 LLMs are confidently wrong 10-20% of the time, and those mistakes are only getting harder to catch to the untrained eyes. They're obviously here to stay since they enable fast, "cheap" code, but because of this, we're heading toward a legal industry model where a few highly sought-after experts handle the real depth, heavily augmented by Al. A bimodal distribution where the majority struggle. 
 Managing these tools is taking all the fun out of coding. A lot of senior/staff+ ICs I talk to, myself included, are looking to hit FIRE early and exit the workforce sooner rather than later. The pipeline for training new replacements is already eroded, and long term, this is going to create a massive gap for anyone who actually has the technical depth to step up. Either that, or we achieve true AGI in the next 10-20 years, and then having a job would be the least of our worries...

Stuck in my career. Please help.

Quick context. I'm 29. I have a bit over 500K passively invested in index funds compounding at around 10%/year and maybe like 5K in savings (this is in CAD currency). Unemployment ended a few months ago which is why I'm running low on savings.
 I'm starting my new job this month in Ontario, Canada making 75K/year (or 69K/year if my negotiation doesn't go through) and I'm not really sure where to go from here with my career and to make more money.
 I've been a software developer for four years and I have an unrelated bachelor's degree and related diploma but I suck at software development and getting re-hired besides my new job has been near impossible (even for intern level summer jobs!) because I never took my career seriously until now. I might as well be at intern level skill-wise but without the excuse of "I'm a university student" to incentivize hiring at that level.
 My highest salary was $115K as a contractor in the private sector as a support specialist which happened by luck through a recommendation of a friend of family, but at my last job with the government as a software developer, my salary was $89K/year. Unfortunately, my contract ended without being renewed because of budget cuts, and I was unemployed for just about a year.
 During my unemployment, even with time spent prepping, I failed literally over 35 technical interviews up until I got this job at the same department through networking. Even when negotiating my salary, it dropped down to $75K/year from what it was before (and may even be lower than that).
 Being unemployed for so long humbled me because I assumed I'd be able to find a job quickly and would get an above six figure salary automatically based on years of experience. Especially when seeing most of my colleagues maintaining their 100k-200k/year salaries and even getting bigger bonuses and promotions. Clearly, the job market disagreed with my expectations and skill level and I'm more motivated than ever to improve my skills. 
 But a year of rejection has reasonably and justifiably nuked my confidence as a software developer. Near the end of my unemployment, I literally reached a point of desperation of even being willing to take a 50K/year job (which wasn't even guaranteed btw) working in support or even an unrelated field doing something in customer service.
 At one point, I was considering whether to just go into sales and start doing door-to-door or just SOMETHING that could make me some form of income and potentially scale to a six figure or higher salary in a few years as long as I put in the hours and show up. But I'm not sure how much of this is just me fantasizing without having to actually test it right away or an actual grounded path. Especially since I already invested so much into being a software developer and also need money in the meantime to sustain my living costs since I don't want to liquidate my investments. But the future of tech seems bleak.
 Given my salary for my new job, and how expensive the cost of living is in my city, living single on my salary will be basically almost paycheck to paycheck. If I end up wanting to get married and having kids in a few years, I want at least double my current salary for it to make sense for me financially.
 So with my new job, I can work hard to get a permanent position. In 5 years, I'll automatically get back to my old salary (~90K) at my current position since it happens automatically with the government. I can also aim for the next level sooner and apply and get promoted (still quite difficult in the current job market) and the next level would jump me to 90K+/year starting salary at that new permanent government position, and I'd be getting a 3K annual raise from there. Getting an online master's degree could help with this.
 I do need active income regardless right now, so I'm going to be working hard to learn and improve in this new position, but I just feel stuck.
 Is sales viable as a side gig and potentially a main future source of income? Should I just lock in fully on this government job? Given how poorly I was interviewing with the private sector as a software developer, is it even worth more energy? 
 Any suggestions would be appreciated.

Why am I working more if AI was supposed to make coding easier?

I have over nine years of experience in ML and have always worked hard to keep up with the industry, but for the past year and a half, I’ve been working to the point of burnout.
 Over the last year or so i am and most of my friends and colleagues are working 10–12 hours a day, six days a week as companies have shifted to being "AI-first" or "AI-native," it is absolutely contrary to the claim that AI would make developers' lives easier and cut down on work time—the exact opposite is happening. 
 This is happening partly because we constantly have to learn new AI-related development tools, and partly because management pressures us to speed things up. Of course, no one can say no; we’ve already been through one round of layoffs and are expecting another—and I don’t need to tell you how hard it is to find a job right now. So, people are desperately clinging to their jobs and grinding away late into the night, terrified of falling behind the market or underperforming and getting fired.
 Ultimately I has a feeling this productivity boost has less to do with AI but more with a overtime. Is it like this for everyone, or did I just get unlucky?

Software engineer job postings ask for mentoring more than Kubernetes. We counted 3,518 postings to check

We pulled every open posting from 81 companies' public Greenhouse boards for seven roles and counted which words actually show up. 3,518 postings in total. Some of it surprised us.
 Software engineer postings mention mentoring more often than Kubernetes or React. Almost half of them do. Python, the most common language, comes in just below that.
 Product manager postings say "roadmap" in more than 85% of cases. Jira? Seven out of 421. Marketing looks the same: Google Ads came up six times in 347 postings, while "pipeline" is in over half.
 Every time we could compare the two, postings named the practice, not the tool. Observability, not Grafana. SIEM, not Splunk.
 So if your resume is mostly a list of tools, it might be missing the words the posting actually uses.
 Big caveat: mostly tech companies, one ATS vendor. Sales, cybersecurity, DevOps and accounting are here too: https://www.zoevera.com/resume/ats-resume-keyword-study

Completed Airbnb's Staff+ loop - here are my thoughts

EDIT: Removed the links to the tagged questions since many people seem hung up on this being a potential ad. I understand, we're all tired of ads. Now back to the aim of this post, providing clarity on the process.
 Summary
 I just completed Airbnb's Staff+ loop recently and I want to share some thoughts about the process, the timeline, my preparation strategy and feelings about the future as I wait for the result.
 Background
 I have interviewed with Airbnb for a senior role about five years ago and bombed so bad in the very first round that it made me question my choice of career.
 This time, a sr recruiter reached out to me on LinkedIn in July and I formally started the interview process soon after that. I believe Airbnb changed its loop structure (not sure if it's for all levels or for staff+ only) during this time so there was some churn on the interview structure as I was going through it.
 Process
 We scheduled a quick phone call to go over the process that looks like this at a high level:
   Round Format Notes    HM Screen (1x) 60 minutes; a mid-level conversation about my work ex., preferred areas of work, team's area of work, short to mid term challenges the team faces etc. It is my belief that beyond helping Airbnb decide if they should spend time interviewing me, it also helps decide the level I should continue interviewing for.   Architecture (2x) 60 minutes; 1 system design problem, few follow up questions on scaling, edge cases, CAP theorem tradeoffs etc. What I found most interesting was that they turned out to be super engaging conversations between two staff+ engineers about interesting edge cases in the given problem and clever optimizations one could add. The actual diagramming I did was super minimal and I was told not to worry about it since the conversation is going in the "right" direction.   Experience Interview (1x) 60 minutes; a low-level conversation with a staff+ engineer about my work experience in general and up to two long-running, large-scale projects specifically. I always have two slide decks (with diagrams) lying around to explain two of my recent/favorite projects. It also helps that one of the large features I've shipped is publicly used by about 2 billion MAUs so I use that as a "live" demo, too! The conversation then went deep into all the real-life sharding issues, and operational concerns one deals with at that scale.   Coding (1x) 45 minutes; a heavily modified version of a popular problem tagged to Airbnb. I was able to quickly solve the problem, clear the edge cases and get it to run. We spent the rest of the time optimizing it for runtime and discussed how something like this could be deployed in production.   Core Values (x1) 60 minutes; a behavioral round seen through the lens of Airbnb's core values. This turned out to be more deep and personal than any interview I've taken or given. Very interesting!   Timeline
 I had a great time managing the timeline for this loop. I really appreciated the level of flexibility Airbnb offers candidates. You get your own portal where you can track and manage your interview process with them. You can request reschedules (latest by an hour before the interview) and push interviews away as far as you need.
 Preparation Strategy
 Preparing for this loop felt really smooth compared to some of the loops I've given before. Something that really helped this time around was the sheer of volume of interviews I've conducted on behalf of my current employer. I got really used to the process, its stated claims, and ways to optimize those 60 minutes from one side of the desk, that it made the other side very approachable.
 I did not prepare for my architecture interviews at all. One of my unpopular opinions is that any staff+ engineer should be able to give an architecture interview in a moment's notice. It's very simply a narrow application of something you ought to be doing everyday at work, at least ideally.
 I always go back to this video by Jackson Gabbard as my foundation for preparing for behavioral interviews and this time was no different.
 For the coding rounds, I focused on the Airbnb tagged questions. This was very helpful.
 I would also recommend this sequence of processing coding problems as it really helped me:
  Verbally explain the naive solution (e.g. to pick the Kth largest element, we could simply sort this array and pick the Kth element from the end) and why you wouldn't want to implement that.
 Write down your proposed solution as a multi-line code comment. If possible, outline possible edge cases or rooms for optimization right away.
 Write down the key steps of your algorithm as single line code comments and get buy-in.
 Write actual code by expanding the single line comments into actual code.
 Perform a dry-run and keep optimizing as much as the time allows.
  Closing Thoughts
 I had a great time preparing for and giving these interviews. I am optimistic about receiving a hire decision but not very sure about the leveling (I'm staff now but would like to land Sr Staff). But nothing is guaranteed until I get the news. Time to enjoy not having to grind PracHub and crack open a cold one.
 Happy to answer your questions but please do not DM me.

UPDATE: Head of Engineering Lied About PIP

I'm still in disbelief. Losing my last job ended up being a blessing for me.
 I managed to get some good severance, and collected unemployment. Applied to 100+ jobs, had a good 8+ interview loops scheduled and just landed another job.
 I went through the interview loop at 3 companies, getting rejected from two of them but landing the third.
 Ended up getting a better job, with a higher TC, better name recognition with better career opportunities.
 Weeks ago I was honestly completely despondent. I've sat at my desk and cried multiple times. The stories I read online of people applying for hundreds of jobs, no interviews and being unemployed for over a year terrified me. I thought my career was almost over.
 I hope this serves as motivation for someone that losing your job isn't always bad. Sometimes it's exactly what you need. If my stupid ass can get a better job, I'm sure you can too. 
 It's okay to be scared for the interview and feel unprepared. Screw it, just do it anyways. There's almost nothing to lose, if you bomb it there's always next time.
 Aside: I learned a valuable personal lesson. When I was studying for the final round interview for my last job that let me go, my grandmother was in the hospital and not doing well.
 I pushed off going to see her until the day before my interview. I was then told she didn't have much time left. When I finally went to see her, she wasn't able to communicate with me. I ended up sleeping on the floor in front of her bed until she ultimately passed away.
 I wasted the last week I could have had with my grandmother for a piece of shit job that treated me like trash and threw me away like I was nothing.
 I'll probably never get over that mistake, but I hope other people don't make the same mistake as me. 
 A job is a job, they don't actually care about you. You can always get another job, you can't always get back some moments in your life.
